justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over longer horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 1330 is anchored primarily to recent price action and momentum, assuming no major overnight catalysts materialize. Markets tend to exhibit mean-reversion at very short horizons when no strong directional signal is present, so I kept the one-day estimate close to the prevailing level. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher to 1335, incorporating a mild positive drift assumption consistent with longer-run trend behavior. The one-month estimate of 1345 reflects a continuation of that gentle upward bias, though the increment is deliberately modest given how quickly macro conditions can shift over a four-week window.

The confidence interval widths widen progressively across horizons, which is a standard feature of forecasting under uncertainty — more time means more opportunity for surprises to accumulate. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 37 points reflects typical intraday and overnight volatility. By one week, the interval expands to about plus or minus 65 points, capturing the potential for a few days of correlated moves in either direction driven by data releases or sentiment shifts. At one month, the interval of plus or minus 125 points accounts for the full range of plausible macro developments, earnings news, and positioning changes that could meaningfully reprice the asset over that period.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharp inflation surprise, a central bank policy shock, or a sudden tightening in credit conditions — could drive prices well below the lower bounds. Geopolitical escalation or a systemic financial stress event, while not the base case, could produce tail moves that exceed even the stated 90% intervals. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected growth or earnings surprise, a dovish policy pivot, or a significant short-covering rally could push prices above the upper bounds faster than the gradual drift embedded in my point estimates.

It is also worth noting that these intervals are constructed under an implicit assumption of relatively normal market functioning. If liquidity deteriorates significantly — as can happen around major risk events or quarter-end periods — realized volatility could spike in ways that make even the one-day interval appear too narrow. My estimates are best understood as probabilistic summaries of the central tendency of outcomes rather than hard boundaries, and any single macro or geopolitical catalyst with sufficient surprise content could render them obsolete quickly.
